title: Balaam's donkey (Numbers 22:21–35)
hook: a donkey sees the angel her master can't, and speaks

segments.voice: Yesterday, twelve spies, a cluster of grapes on a pole, and Caleb saying we are well able. Your line was we're not grasshoppers. What did you step toward? Day four hundred five.

A king named Balak is frightened. A huge people has camped on his border, the Israelites, fresh from the desert. So he sends for a famous seer named Balaam, a man known for blessings and curses that stick. Come and curse this people for me, he says, and I'll pay you well. Balaam saddles his donkey and sets out. And this is where the Bible tells one of its funniest, strangest stories. On the road, the donkey suddenly swerves into a field. Balaam beats her back onto the road. Then she squeezes against a wall and crushes his foot. He beats her again. Then she just lies down under him. And Balaam, furious, beats her a third time.
screen: `A KING HIRES A CURSE.` → `THE DONKEY SWERVES, SQUEEZES, LIES DOWN.` → `THREE BEATINGS.`

segments.voice: Then this, in the King James Bible: "And the LORD opened the mouth of the ass, and she said unto Balaam, What have I done unto thee, that thou hast smitten me these three times?" And here's the funny part: Balaam argues back. He doesn't seem surprised that his donkey is talking. You've made a fool of me, he says. If I had a sword I'd kill you. And she answers, reasonably: haven't I carried you all your life? Have I ever done this before? And he has to admit, no. "Then the LORD opened the eyes of Balaam, and he saw the angel of the LORD standing in the way, and his sword drawn in his hand." The donkey had seen it all along, three times. The famous seer, the professional who sees what others can't, is the only one on the road who's blind. And his donkey saved his life. The angel says so: if she hadn't turned aside, I would have killed you and let her live. The rest of the story is just as surprising. Balaam goes on to King Balak, climbs the hills three times to curse Israel, and three times blessing comes out of his mouth instead. One of those blessings, how goodly are thy tents, O Jacob, is still said in Jewish morning prayers. And in 1967, archaeologists in Jordan found a plaster inscription from around the eighth century before Christ that names Balaam son of Beor as a seer of the gods. He was remembered outside the Bible too. The lesson Christians have long drawn: God can speak through anyone. Even a donkey.
screen: `WHAT HAVE I DONE UNTO THEE?` · `THE SEER IS THE ONE WHO'S BLIND.` · `THE CURSE COMES OUT A BLESSING.` · `HIS NAME ON A WALL IN JORDAN.` · then, large: `THE LORD OPENED THE MOUTH OF THE ASS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to an unlikely messenger. Settle, and breathe. Think of the voices in your life you tend to brush off. A child who says something too blunt. A coworker you don't respect much. A critic. A stranger. Your own tired body, lying down under you in the road. Has one of them been trying to tell you something, maybe more than once? Picture yourself stopping, getting off the donkey, and actually listening. If you pray, you can ask to have your eyes opened like Balaam's. The bell holds the time.
Balaam's donkey. She saw the angel in the road three times, while her famous master saw nothing, and then she spoke.
Your line: even a donkey can see. Today, take one piece of advice seriously from someone you'd normally ignore. Day four hundred five.

howItsDone: Christians often tell Balaam's story to children for its humor and to adults as a reminder that God can speak through unlikely voices; the New Testament mentions Balaam and his donkey in 2 Peter.

fork.setup: you're Balaam. your donkey has swerved, crushed your foot and lain down in the road, and now she's talking to you. what do you do?
fork.reveal: he argues: you've made a fool of me. only after God opens his eyes does he see the angel the donkey saw all along.

original.note: Hebrew: Balaam. His name also appears in an ancient inscription from Deir Alla, in Jordan.

trapdoor: what you thought: a kids' story about a talking animal.
what it means: the professional seer is the only one blind on the road; God speaks through a donkey and turns a curse into a blessing.
what a scholar hears: Balaam son of Beor, named in the Deir Alla plaster inscription, and 'how goodly are thy tents', still said in Jewish morning prayer.

notes: Deir Alla inscription: discovered 1967 at Tell Deir Alla, Jordan; generally dated to the ninth or eighth century BC; it calls Balaam son of Beor 'a seer of the gods'. Confirm the dating phrase 'around the eighth century before Christ'.
Mah Tovu (Numbers 24:5) opens the Jewish morning service in many prayer books; confirm.
The script follows Numbers 22:21–35 without addressing why God is angry after permitting the trip (22:20 vs 22:22), a known puzzle; consider a note.
Later tradition is harder on Balaam (Numbers 31:16; 2 Peter 2:15; Revelation 2:14); the script doesn't go there.
